question.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=2\sqrt{3-t}\,i+(1-2t)\,j+(t+3)\,k$ at the point $P(2,-3,5).$
question.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,-3,5)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point, the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i-3\,j+5\,k \\ 2\sqrt{3-t}\,i+(1-2t)\,j+(t+3)\,k & =2\,i-3\,j+5\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3-t}=2 \\ 1-2t=-3 \\ t+3=5\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $t=2.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,-3,5)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(2).$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{3-t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+3)\,k \\  & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3-t}}\,i-2\,j+k \\ {r}^{′}(2) & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3-2}}\,i-2\,j+k \\  & =-\,i-2\,j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point $P(2,-3,5)$ is $-\,i-2\,j+k.$

At the point where $t=0$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(0)$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{e}^{t},\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{e}^{-t},\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,-{e}^{-t},\,2t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨{e}^{0},\,-{e}^{-0},\,2\cdot 0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=0$ is $⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩.$

question.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+1),1-5t⟩$ at the point where $t=0,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
question.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=0,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(0)$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(0)+u{r}^{′}(0),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+1),1-5(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+1)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-5t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+1},-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0) & =⟨\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+1},-5⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=0$ is

$$
R(u)=⟨0,1⟩+u⟨0,-5⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

question.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ at the point where $t=\pi ,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
question.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\pi ,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(\pi )+u{r}^{′}(\pi ),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\pi ) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=\pi $ is

$$
R(u)=⟨-1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

question.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+2t,4-{t}^{2}⟩,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨0,-1⟩.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t+2,-2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $⟨0,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨0,-1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨0,-1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨0,-1⟩\cdot ⟨2t+2,-2t⟩ & =0 \\ 0(2t+2)+(-1)(-2t) & =0 \\ 2t & =0 \\ t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{2}+2(0),4-{0}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨0,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(0,4).$

question.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=(t+2)\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
question.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1})\,j \\  & =i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [(t+2)\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,j]\cdot (i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}\,j) & =0 \\ (t+2)\cdot 1+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}} & =0 \\ t+2+t & =0 \\ 2t+2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=-1.$ 

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1)=(-1+2)\,i+\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+1}\,j=i+\sqrt{2}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(1,\sqrt{2}).$

question.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-2t\,,\,{t}^{2}\,,\,8t-2{t}^{2}⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8t-2{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t-2,\,2t,\,8-4t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c\,⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c\,⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨2t-2,\,2t,\,8-4t⟩ & =c\,⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨2t-2,\,2t,\,8-4t⟩ & =⟨c\,,\,2c\,,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2t-2=c \\ 2t=2c \\ 8-4t=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we obtain that $t=2.$ Substituting to the second equation, we get $c=2.$
These values also satisfy the first equation. 

Therefore, $⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=2.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨{2}^{2}-2(2)\,,\,{2}^{2}\,,\,8(2)-2(2)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,4,\,8⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(0,4,8).$

question.problem: Given the curve $r(t)={e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
question.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =c(2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =2c{e}^{2t}\,i+c(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j$ gives:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}=2c{e}^{2t} \\ {t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2}=c(2t+1)\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain $c=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting $c=\frac{1}{2}$ into the second equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(2t+1) \\ {t}^{2} & =0 \\ t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel at the point corresponding to $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & ={e}^{0}\,i+({0}^{2}+0+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =i+\frac{1}{2}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$
